title: Slavery and the Burning Bush
subtitle: Exodus 1 to 4, Berean Standard Bible
description: Israel’s oppression, Moses’ rescue and calling, and his return to Egypt.
paragraphs: Genesis ended with a coffin in Egypt. Exodus begins with the family that coffin left behind.

The sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob are named again: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. Joseph was already in Egypt. The whole family line numbered seventy persons, and then that generation died. Joseph died. His brothers died. Their generation passed, but their descendants did not shrink into the land that had taken them in.
The Israelites were fruitful in Egypt. They increased rapidly, multiplied, and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them.

Then the throne changed hands. "Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt." The new Pharaoh did not see a family brought there by famine and kept alive by Joseph's wisdom. He saw a people growing inside his borders. He told his people that the Israelites had become much too numerous for them. If war broke out, Pharaoh feared Israel might join Egypt's enemies, fight against Egypt, and leave the land.

Egypt answered growth with force. The Egyptians put slave masters over Israel to oppress them with forced labor. Israel built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. But the more the Egyptians oppressed them, the more Israel multiplied and spread, until the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. They made Israel work ruthlessly. They made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar and with all kinds of work in the fields. Every service they imposed was harsh.
When labor did not stop the growth, Pharaoh reached for the newborn sons.

He spoke to the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah. When they helped the Hebrew women give birth, they were to watch on the delivery stool. If the child was a son, they were to kill him. If the child was a daughter, she could live.
"The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live."

Pharaoh called the midwives in and demanded to know why they had let the boys live. The midwives answered that the Hebrew women were not like the Egyptian women. They were vigorous and gave birth before a midwife arrived. God dealt well with the midwives because they feared Him, and the people multiplied and became very strong. God gave the midwives families of their own.
Pharaoh widened the order. He commanded all his people: "Every son born to the Hebrews you must throw into the Nile, but every daughter you may allow to live."

In that Egypt, a Levite man married a Levite woman. She conceived and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months. She could hide him no longer, so she took a papyrus basket, coated it with tar and pitch, placed the child in it, and put it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile. The child's sister stood at a distance to learn what would happen to him.

Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the Nile while her attendants walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her slave girl to get it. She opened it and saw the baby. He was crying. She had pity on him and said this was one of the Hebrew children.

Then the baby's sister came forward. She asked Pharaoh's daughter whether she should go and call a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for her. Pharaoh's daughter told her to go. The girl went and called the child's mother. Pharaoh's daughter told the mother to take the child and nurse him for her, and she would pay her wages. The woman took the child and nursed him.
The hidden baby was now being nursed by his own mother, and Pharaoh's daughter was paying her wages.
When the child grew older, his mother brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses and explained, "I drew him out of the water."

Moses grew up as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, but Exodus first shows him as a grown man when he goes out to his own people and looks on their burdens. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. Moses looked this way and that way. Seeing no one, he struck the Egyptian down and hid him in the sand.

The next day Moses went out again and saw two Hebrews fighting. He spoke to the one who was in the wrong and asked why he was striking his companion. The man answered by naming Moses' secret. He asked who had made Moses ruler and judge over them. He asked if Moses planned to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian. Moses was afraid. The thing he had done had become known.
When Pharaoh heard about it, he tried to kill Moses. Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian.

A runaway from Pharaoh's house sat down by a well in Midian. The priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father's flock. Shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and rescued them. Then he watered their flock himself.

The daughters returned to their father, Reuel, earlier than expected. He asked how they had come home so soon that day. They told him an Egyptian had rescued them from the shepherds and had even drawn water for them and watered the flock. Reuel asked where the man was and why they had left him outside. He told his daughters to call him so he could eat bread.
Moses agreed to stay with the man. Reuel gave Moses his daughter Zipporah in marriage. She gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying he had been a foreigner in a strange land.
During that long period, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned because of their slavery and cried out. Their cry for help rose up to God from their slavery.
"So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God saw the Israelites and took notice."

Moses was still in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. There the angel of the LORD appeared to Moses in a blazing fire from within a bush. "Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed."

Moses said he would go over and see this strange sight, why the bush did not burn up. When the LORD saw that Moses had gone over to look, God called to him from within the bush and said his name twice. Moses answered that he was there.
"Do not come any closer," God said. "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground."
Then God named Himself as the God of Moses' father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.

The LORD said, "I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings. I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey."
The mission reached Moses in the same breath. God would send him to Pharaoh so Moses could bring the Israelites out of Egypt.

Moses answered with the size of his own name. Who was he that he should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt? God answered, "I will surely be with you." The sign would come after obedience had already started: when Moses had brought the people out of Egypt, they would worship God on that same mountain.
Moses asked another question. If he went to the Israelites and told them the God of their fathers had sent him, they might ask God's name. What should he tell them?
God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"

God also told Moses to say that the LORD, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, had sent him. This was God's name forever, the name by which He was to be remembered in every generation.

Moses was to assemble the elders of Israel and tell them the LORD had appeared to him. God had seen what had been done to Israel in Egypt. He promised to bring them up out of their misery into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey. The elders would listen. Then Moses and the elders were to go to the king of Egypt and ask to make a three-day journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifices to the LORD their God.

God also told Moses that the king of Egypt would not let Israel go unless compelled by a mighty hand. God would stretch out His hand and strike Egypt with all His wonders. After that, Pharaoh would let them go. Israel would not leave empty-handed. God would make the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the Israelites, and the Hebrew women would ask their Egyptian neighbors for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. In that way they would plunder the Egyptians.
Moses still had objections.

He answered that the Israelites might not believe him or listen to his voice. They might say the LORD had not appeared to him. The LORD asked what was in Moses' hand. Moses said it was a staff. God told him to throw it on the ground. Moses threw it down, and it became a snake. He ran from it. God told him to reach out his hand and take it by the tail. Moses did, and the snake became a staff again in his hand. God gave the sign so Israel would believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, had appeared to Moses.

God gave a second sign. Moses put his hand into his cloak and took it out leprous, like snow. He put it back into his cloak and took it out restored, like the rest of his flesh. If Israel did not believe the first sign, they might believe the second. If they still did not believe, Moses was to take some water from the Nile, pour it on the dry ground, and the water would become blood.

Moses answered again. He had never been eloquent, not in the past and not since God had spoken to him. He was slow of speech and tongue. The LORD answered that He had made man's mouth. He made the mute, the deaf, the seeing, and the blind. He told Moses to go, and He would help Moses speak and teach him what to say.
Moses asked God to send someone else.

The anger of the LORD burned against Moses. God named Aaron, Moses' brother, a Levite who spoke well and was already on his way to meet Moses. Aaron would be glad when he saw him. Moses was to speak to Aaron and put the words in his mouth. God would help both of them speak and teach them what to do. Aaron would speak to the people for Moses. Aaron would be Moses' spokesman, and Moses would be like God to Aaron. Moses was also to take the staff in his hand, the staff with which he would perform the signs.
Moses went back to Jethro, his father-in-law, and asked to return to his own people in Egypt to see if they were still alive. Jethro told him to go in peace.

The LORD told Moses in Midian to return to Egypt, for all the men who had wanted to kill him were dead. Moses took his wife and sons, mounted them on a donkey, and started back to Egypt. Moses took the staff of God in his hand.

On the road back, the LORD gave Moses the warning he was to carry into Pharaoh's court. Moses was to perform before Pharaoh all the wonders God had given him the power to do. But God would harden Pharaoh's heart so he would not let the people go. Moses was to tell Pharaoh that Israel was the LORD's firstborn son. If Pharaoh refused to let God's son go to serve Him, God would kill Pharaoh's firstborn son.

At a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him. Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched it to Moses' feet. She called Moses a bridegroom of blood. Then the LORD let him alone.

The LORD told Aaron to go into the wilderness to meet Moses. Aaron went and met Moses at the mountain of God and kissed him. Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD who had sent him and all the signs He had commanded him to do.

So Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites. Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and Moses performed the signs in the sight of the people. And they believed.
When the Israelites heard that the LORD had attended to them and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped.

The man who had fled Egypt had come back carrying a staff, a brother spokesman, and a message for Pharaoh. The people under the brick pits had heard that God had seen their misery. In front of Moses now stood the court where he had once been a son of the house.

title: Let My People Go
subtitle: Exodus 5 to 10, Berean Standard Bible
description: Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, the heavier labor, and the first nine plagues.
paragraphs: The elders believed. Moses had come back to Egypt with Aaron beside him, a staff in his hand, and a word from the mountain of God. Now that word had to enter Pharaoh's court.
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.'"
Pharaoh answered, "Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go."
That question would hang over everything that followed. Pharaoh did not know the LORD. Egypt was about to learn His name by signs, plagues, and a land brought low.

Moses and Aaron told Pharaoh that the God of the Hebrews had met with them. They asked to go three days into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD their God, or He might strike them with plague or with the sword. The king of Egypt called them trouble for the labor force. Why were Moses and Aaron taking the people away from their work?
Then Pharaoh made the work harder.

That same day he commanded the slave drivers and the Israelite foremen. They were no longer to supply the people with straw for making bricks as they had done before. The Israelites had to go and gather straw for themselves. But the quota of bricks stayed the same. Pharaoh said the Israelites were idle, and that was why they kept crying out to go and sacrifice to their God. "Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies."

The people scattered through Egypt to gather stubble for straw. The slave drivers pressed them to finish the daily work as when straw was given. The Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's slave drivers had set over the people, were beaten and asked why they had not met the brick tally either yesterday or today.

The foremen went to Pharaoh and cried out. Why was he treating his servants this way? No straw was given to them, yet they were told to make bricks. Their servants were beaten, but the fault belonged to Pharaoh's own people. Pharaoh called them idle again. Idle. That was why they wanted to go and sacrifice to the LORD. They were to get back to work. No straw would be given, and they would still deliver the full number of bricks.

As the foremen came out from Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron waiting to speak with them. The men turned the weight of the day onto the brothers. "May the LORD look upon you and judge you," they said, "for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!"

Moses returned to the LORD with the failure in his hands. Pharaoh had brought more trouble on the people since Moses had gone to speak in God's name. Moses said, "You have not delivered Your people in any way."

The LORD answered Moses with the future Pharaoh had not yet seen. "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh, for because of My mighty hand he will let the people go; because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land."

God spoke His name again. He was the LORD. He had appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but He had not made Himself known to them by His name the LORD in the way He was now doing with Moses. He had established His covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners. He had heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians kept in slavery. He had remembered His covenant.

Moses was to tell Israel: "I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God."
God also promised to bring them into the land He had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to give it to them as a possession.
Moses spoke those words to the Israelites, but they did not listen to him. Their spirits were broken, and their slavery was cruel.

The LORD told Moses to go and tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to let the Israelites leave his land. Moses answered that the Israelites had not listened to him. How would Pharaoh listen to him, Moses, who was faltering in speech? Then the text slows down and names the family through whom the command would move. Amram married Jochebed, and she bore Aaron and Moses. Aaron married Elisheba, and she bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. It was this Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said to bring the Israelites out of Egypt by their divisions.
When Moses and Aaron went back to Pharaoh, Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three.

God made the terms plain to Moses. He had made Moses like God to Pharaoh, and Aaron would be his prophet. Pharaoh's heart would be hardened. God would multiply His signs and wonders in Egypt, and Pharaoh would not listen until God laid His hand on Egypt and brought Israel out with mighty acts of judgment.
First came the sign in court.

Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did as the LORD commanded. "Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a serpent." Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers. The Egyptian magicians did the same by their secret arts. Each man threw down his staff, and the staffs became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs. Pharaoh's heart was hardened anyway, and he would not listen, just as the LORD had said.

The next morning Moses met Pharaoh at the water. Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials, "and all the water was turned to blood." The fish in the Nile died. The river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink its water. Blood was throughout the land of Egypt, in rivers, canals, ponds, and pools. The Egyptian magicians did the same by their secret arts, and Pharaoh's heart was hardened. He turned and went into his palace. The Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the river water. Seven full days passed after the LORD struck the Nile.
Then the LORD sent frogs.

Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land. They entered Pharaoh's palace, his bedroom, and his bed. They entered the houses of his officials and his people, the ovens and kneading bowls. The magicians also made frogs come up on the land by their secret arts.

This time Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron. He asked them to pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from him and his people, and he said he would let the people go to offer sacrifices to the LORD. Moses let Pharaoh set the time. Pharaoh said tomorrow. Moses said it would be as Pharaoh said, so that he would know there was no one like the LORD their God. The frogs would leave the houses, courtyards, and fields. Only the frogs in the Nile would remain.

Moses cried out to the LORD about the frogs He had brought on Pharaoh. The frogs died in the houses, courtyards, and fields. The Egyptians gathered them into piles, and the land stank. When Pharaoh saw there was relief, he hardened his heart and would not listen.

The LORD told Moses to tell Aaron to stretch out his staff and strike the dust of the ground, and it became gnats throughout Egypt. Gnats were on people and animals. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. They told Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen.
Then came flies.

The LORD set Goshen apart. "But on that day I will give special treatment to the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there." Thick swarms entered Pharaoh's palace and the houses of his officials. Throughout Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms. Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and told them to go and sacrifice to their God within the land. Moses said that would not be right. The sacrifices Israel offered would be detestable to the Egyptians, and if the Egyptians saw them, they might stone Israel. Israel had to go three days into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD their God as He commanded.

Pharaoh said he would let them go to sacrifice in the wilderness, but only if they did not go very far away. He told Moses to pray for him. Moses prayed, and the LORD removed the swarms from Pharaoh, from his officials, and from his people. Not one remained. But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also and would not let the people go.

Next the LORD struck Egypt's livestock in the field: horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. The next day the LORD did it. "All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died." Pharaoh sent men to investigate and saw that not one of Israel's animals had died. Yet Pharaoh's heart was unyielding, and he would not let the people go.

Then Moses took handfuls of soot from a furnace and threw it into the air in Pharaoh's sight. It became fine dust over all the land of Egypt and caused festering boils to break out on people and animals. The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils. The boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians. The LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not listen, just as the LORD had said to Moses.

Before the next plague, Moses carried a warning. Early in the morning he stood before Pharaoh and told him to let God's people go. This time God could have struck Pharaoh and his people with a plague that would wipe them off the earth. Instead, for this reason God had raised Pharaoh up: to show him His power, and so that God's name might be proclaimed in all the earth. At this time tomorrow, God would send the worst hailstorm that had ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now.

Moses told Pharaoh's officials and people to bring their servants and livestock in from the field. Whoever remained in the field would die when the hail fell. Some of Pharaoh's officials feared the word of the LORD and hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter. Those who ignored the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field.

Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky. The LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning flashed down to the ground. The hail struck down everything in the fields, people and animals alike, and it beat down every plant and stripped every tree. Only in Goshen, where the Israelites were, was there no hail.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. "This time I have sinned," he said. "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." He asked them to pray. There had been enough thunder and hail. He would let the people go. They would stay no longer.

Moses told Pharaoh that as soon as he left the city, he would spread out his hands in prayer to the LORD. The thunder would stop and there would be no more hail, so Pharaoh might know that the earth is the LORD's. Still, Moses said, he knew Pharaoh and his officials did not yet fear the LORD God.

Moses left Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail stopped, and the rain no longer poured down on the land. When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he sinned again. He and his officials hardened their hearts. Pharaoh would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

Pharaoh's own officials finally spoke against him. They asked, "How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt lies in ruins?"

Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. Pharaoh told them to go and worship the LORD their God, then asked who would be going. Moses said Israel would go with young and old, with sons and daughters, with flocks and herds, because they were to celebrate a festival to the LORD. Pharaoh said the LORD would be with them if he ever let them go with their women and children. He could see that they were bent on evil. "No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting." Moses and Aaron were driven from Pharaoh's presence.

Then Moses stretched out his staff over Egypt, and the LORD made an east wind blow across the land all that day and all that night. By morning the wind had brought locusts. They invaded all Egypt and settled down in every area of the country. The ground was black with them. They devoured everything growing in the fields and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green remained on tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.

Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron. He said he had sinned against the LORD their God and against them. He asked them to forgive his sin once more and pray that the LORD would take this deadly plague away. Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD. The LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind, which caught up the locusts and carried them into the Red Sea. Not a locust was left anywhere in Egypt. But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.

Then darkness came over Egypt, darkness that could be felt. Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and total darkness covered all Egypt for three days. "No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings."

Pharaoh summoned Moses and told him to go and worship the LORD. Even the women and children could go. Only the flocks and herds had to stay behind. Moses said Israel's livestock had to go with them too, because from them they had to take animals for sacrifices and burnt offerings to the LORD their God. Their animals would go with them. Not a hoof would be left behind.
The LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he was not willing to let them go.
Pharaoh said to Moses, "Depart from me! Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die."
Moses answered, "As you say, I will never see your face again."

Pharaoh had asked at the beginning who the LORD was. By the time Moses left his presence, Egypt had been struck in its river, its homes, its dust, its air, its fields, its sky, and its light. The question had been answered in judgment after judgment. Still Pharaoh would not bow.

title: Passover and the Sea
subtitle: Exodus 11 to 15, Berean Standard Bible
description: Passover, departure from Egypt, the sea crossing, and the first wilderness waters.
paragraphs: Egypt had seen the Nile turn to blood. Frogs had filled the houses. Gnats had come from the dust. Flies had blackened Pharaoh's palace. Livestock had died, boils had broken out, hail had flattened the fields, locusts had eaten what the hail left, and darkness had covered the land for three days.
Pharaoh still would not let Israel go.

The LORD told Moses there would be one more plague. "I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague. After that, he will allow you to leave this place. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely."

Before Moses left Pharaoh, he announced what that plague would be. About midnight the LORD would go throughout Egypt. Every firstborn son in Egypt would die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle. There would be a great cry throughout Egypt, worse than there had ever been or ever would be again. But among the Israelites, not even a dog would snarl at man or beast. Then Egypt would know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.

Moses told Pharaoh's officials that they would come down to him, bow before him, and say for Israel to get out, he and all the people who followed him. After that, Moses said, he would leave. Then Moses left Pharaoh in hot anger.
Now the LORD prepared Israel for the night that would break Egypt's hold.

The LORD told Moses and Aaron that this month would be the first month of the year for Israel. On the tenth day of the month, each man was to take a lamb for his family, one for each household. If a household was too small to eat a whole lamb, the family was to share one with its nearest neighbor, keeping count of the people and what each could eat. The animals chosen were to be year-old males without defect, taken from the sheep or the goats. They were to be kept until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly of Israel would slaughter them at twilight.

"They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs." That same night they were to eat the meat roasted over the fire, with bitter herbs and bread made without yeast. None of it was to be eaten raw or boiled in water. It was to be roasted over the fire, with the head, legs, and internal organs. None of it was to remain until morning. What remained was to be burned.
"This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD's Passover."

The LORD said that on that night He would pass through Egypt and strike down every firstborn, both people and animals, and bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. "The blood on the houses where you are staying will be a sign; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt."

That day was to be kept as a memorial. Israel would keep it as a lasting ordinance through the generations. For seven days they would eat bread made without yeast. On the first day they would remove yeast from their houses. Anyone who ate anything with yeast in it during those seven days would be cut off from Israel. The first and seventh days would be sacred assemblies. No work was to be done on those days except to prepare food for everyone to eat.

At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as the firstborn of all the livestock. Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was a loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead.

During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. "Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested." He told them to take their flocks and herds as they had said, and go. And he asked them to bless him too.

The Egyptians urged the Israelites to hurry and leave the country, for otherwise, they said, they would all die. So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading troughs wrapped in clothing. The Israelites had done as Moses told them and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. The LORD had made the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the people, and they gave them what they asked for. In that way Israel plundered the Egyptians.

The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth. There were about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. Many other people went up with them as well, and also large droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. With the dough the Israelites had brought from Egypt, they baked loaves of unleavened bread. The dough was without yeast because they had been driven out of Egypt and did not have time to prepare food for themselves.
Now the time the Israelites had lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD's divisions left Egypt.

The people leaving Egypt were not only escaping Pharaoh. They were learning how to remember the night God had brought them out. The LORD set rules for the Passover. No foreigner was to eat it. A slave bought with money could eat it after he had been circumcised. A temporary resident or hired worker could not eat it. The lamb was to be eaten inside a house. None of the meat was to be taken outside. No bone of it was to be broken. The whole community of Israel had to take part. A foreigner living among them who wanted to celebrate the LORD's Passover could do so after all the males in his household had been circumcised. Then he could take part as one born in the land. No uncircumcised person could eat it. The same law applied to the native-born and to the foreigner living among them.

The LORD also claimed Israel's firstborn as His own. Every firstborn, both people and animals, belonged to Him, because by strength of hand He had brought Israel out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. The firstborn of a donkey could be redeemed with a lamb, or its neck was to be broken if it was not redeemed. Every firstborn son among the Israelites was to be redeemed. In days to come, when a son asked his father what this meant, the father was to tell him that the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand. When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let them go, the LORD killed every firstborn in Egypt, both people and animals. That was why Israel sacrificed the firstborn males of every womb to the LORD and redeemed their firstborn sons. The sign would be on Israel's hand and a symbol on Israel's forehead, because the LORD had brought them out of Egypt with His mighty hand.

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the shorter road through the land of the Philistines. God said, "If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt." So God led the people around by the desert road toward the Red Sea. The Israelites left Egypt arrayed for battle.

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him. Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear an oath and had said, "God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place." The promise made in Genesis was moving again. Joseph's coffin was no longer staying behind in Egypt.

From Succoth the Israelites traveled to Etham, at the edge of the desert. By day the LORD went ahead of them in a pillar of cloud to guide them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so they could travel by day or night. Neither pillar left its place in front of the people.

Then the LORD told Moses to have the Israelites turn back and camp near Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal Zephon. Pharaoh would think the Israelites were wandering in confusion and trapped by the desert. God would harden Pharaoh's heart, and Pharaoh would pursue them. But God would gain glory through Pharaoh and his army, and the Egyptians would know that He is the LORD.

The king of Egypt was told that the people had fled. Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them. They asked what they had done in letting the Israelites go from serving them. Pharaoh had his chariot made ready and took his army with him. He took six hundred of the best chariots, along with all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them. The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he pursued the Israelites, who were marching out boldly.

The Egyptians pursued Israel and overtook them as they camped by the sea. When Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up. There were the Egyptians marching toward them. The sea was in front of them. Pharaoh's army was behind them. They were terrified and cried out to the LORD.

They turned on Moses. Had he taken them out to die in the desert because there were no graves in Egypt? What had he done to them by bringing them out of Egypt? Had they not told him in Egypt to leave them alone and let them serve the Egyptians? It would have been better for them to serve Egypt than to die in the desert.

Moses answered the people, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD's salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still."

The LORD told Moses to stop crying out to Him and tell the Israelites to move on. Moses was to raise his staff and stretch out his hand over the sea to divide the water, so the Israelites could go through the sea on dry ground. The Egyptians would follow them into the sea, and God would gain glory through Pharaoh and his whole army, through his chariots and his horsemen. The Egyptians would know that He is the LORD.

The angel of God, who had been traveling in front of Israel's army, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them and stood behind them, coming between the armies of Egypt and Israel. Throughout the night the cloud brought darkness to the one side and light to the other side, so neither went near the other all night long.

Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, "and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided," and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued them. All Pharaoh's horses and chariots and horsemen followed them into the middle of the sea.

During the last watch of the night, the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion. He jammed the wheels of the chariots so they had difficulty driving. The Egyptians said they would get away from the Israelites, because the LORD was fighting for Israel against Egypt.

Then the LORD told Moses to stretch out his hand over the sea so the waters would flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen. Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. The Egyptians tried to flee toward it, but the LORD swept them into the middle of the sea. "The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen, the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived."

But the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. "When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses."

Then Moses and the Israelites sang to the LORD. "The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father's God, and I will exalt Him." They sang that the LORD is a warrior. The LORD is His name. Pharaoh's chariots and his army He had thrown into the sea. The best of Pharaoh's officers were drowned in the Red Sea. The deep waters had covered them, and they sank to the depths like a stone. God's right hand was majestic in power. God's right hand had shattered the enemy.

Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a timbrel in her hand. All the women followed her, with timbrels and dancing. Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea."

After the song, Moses led Israel from the Red Sea into the Desert of Shur. For three days they traveled in the desert without finding water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink its water because it was bitter. That was why the place was called Marah. The people grumbled against Moses, asking what they were to drink.

Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. Moses threw it into the water, and the water became fit to drink. There the LORD gave Israel a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them. He told them that if they listened carefully to His voice and did what was right in His eyes, if they paid attention to His commands and kept all His decrees, He would not bring on them any of the diseases He had brought on the Egyptians, for He is the LORD who heals them.
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Israel camped there near the water.

The people who had once made bricks under Pharaoh's drivers were now camped by springs in the wilderness. Behind them lay Egypt, the dead army on the shore, and the night when God passed through the land. In front of them stood a desert, and over them still stood the cloud and fire of the LORD.

title: Bread, Water, and Amalek
subtitle: Exodus 16 to 18, Berean Standard Bible
description: Manna and quail in the wilderness, water from the rock, Amalek’s attack, and Jethro’s counsel.
paragraphs: Elim had water and shade, but Elim was not the destination. Israel moved on from the springs and palm trees into the Wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai. It was the fifteenth day of the second month after they had come out of Egypt, and the whole congregation was hungry.

Hunger did what Pharaoh's army had not done. It turned Israel back toward Egypt in their own words. The people grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the desert. They said they wished the LORD had killed them in Egypt. In Egypt, they said, they sat around pots of meat and ate all the food they wanted. Now Moses and Aaron had brought them into the desert to starve the whole assembly to death.

Moses and Aaron told all the Israelites that in the evening they would know the LORD had brought them out of Egypt, and in the morning they would see the glory of the LORD. The LORD had heard their grumbling. Their grumbling was not against Moses and Aaron. It was against the LORD.
While Aaron spoke to the whole assembly, they looked toward the wilderness, and there the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.

The LORD told Moses, "I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, 'At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.'"

That evening quail came up and covered the camp. In the morning a layer of dew lay around the camp. When the dew lifted, thin flakes like frost were on the desert ground. "When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, 'What is it?' For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, 'It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.'"

The LORD had already named the test inside the gift. "Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions."

Each person was to gather an omer for each person in his tent. The Israelites did so. Some gathered much, some little. When they measured, the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no shortage. Each had gathered as much as he needed. Moses told them not to keep any of it until morning.

Some did not listen. They kept part of it until morning, and it was full of maggots and stank. Moses was angry with them. Each morning everyone gathered as much as he needed, and when the sun grew hot, what was left on the ground melted away.

On the sixth day the people gathered twice as much, two omers for each person. The leaders came and reported this to Moses. Moses told them what the LORD had commanded. Tomorrow would be a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD. They were to bake what they wanted to bake and boil what they wanted to boil that day, and save whatever was left to be kept until morning. They did as Moses said, and the saved manna did not stink or get maggots in it. On the seventh day the people were to eat what had been saved, because that day was a Sabbath to the LORD. They would find no manna in the field. They were to gather for six days. On the seventh day, the Sabbath, there would be none.

Some people went out on the seventh day to gather anyway, but they found nothing. The LORD asked Moses how long the people would refuse to keep His commands and instructions. The LORD had given them the Sabbath. That was why on the sixth day He gave them bread for two days. Everyone was to stay where he was. No one was to go out on the seventh day. So the people rested on the seventh day.

The house of Israel called the bread manna. "It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey." Moses told Aaron, "Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come." Aaron placed it before the testimony, to be kept, as the LORD commanded. The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land that was settled. They ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan.
From the Wilderness of Sin the whole congregation traveled by stages, as the LORD commanded, and camped at Rephidim. There was no water for the people to drink.

The people quarreled with Moses. They demanded that he give them water to drink. Moses asked why they quarreled with him and why they tested the LORD. But the people thirsted there for water, and they grumbled against Moses. They asked why he had brought them up out of Egypt to kill them, their children, and their livestock with thirst.
Moses cried out to the LORD. What was he to do with these people? They were almost ready to stone him.

The LORD told Moses to go on ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with him. He was to take in his hand the staff with which he struck the Nile, and go. "Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink." Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel.
"He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, 'Is the LORD among us or not?'"
Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.

Moses said to Joshua to choose men for Israel and go out to fight Amalek. The next day Moses would stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in his hand. Joshua did as Moses told him and fought Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. As long as Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.

Moses' hands grew heavy. Aaron and Hur took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron held up one hand and Hur held up the other, so Moses' hands remained steady until sunset. Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.

The LORD told Moses to write this on a scroll as a memorial and recite it in the hearing of Joshua: He would utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner. He said, "a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation."

Now Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, heard of everything God had done for Moses and for Israel, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. Jethro brought Moses' wife Zipporah, who had been sent back, and her two sons. One son was named Gershom, for Moses said he had become a foreigner in a foreign land. The other was named Eliezer, for Moses said the God of his father was his helper and had delivered him from Pharaoh's sword.

Jethro came with Moses' wife and sons into the wilderness where Israel was camped near the mountain of God. Word came to Moses that Jethro was coming, and Moses went out to meet his father-in-law. He bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent.

Moses told Jethro all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel's sake, all the hardships that had met them along the way, and how the LORD had saved them. Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel in rescuing them from Egypt.

Jethro declared, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh, and who has delivered the people from the hand of the Egyptians. Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods, for He did this when they treated Israel with arrogance."
Then Jethro brought a burnt offering and other sacrifices to God. Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law in the presence of God.

The next day Moses sat to judge the people. The people stood around Moses from morning until evening. When Jethro saw all that Moses was doing for the people, he asked what this was and why Moses sat alone while all the people stood around him from morning to evening.
Moses answered that the people came to him to seek God's will. When they had a dispute, they came to him, and he decided between one person and another. He informed them of God's decrees and laws.
Jethro told Moses that what he was doing was not good. Moses and the people who came to him would only wear themselves out. The work was too heavy for Moses. He could not handle it alone.

Jethro gave counsel. Moses was to be the people's representative before God and bring their disputes to Him. He was to teach the Israelites the decrees and laws and show them the way to live and the duties they were to perform. But he was also to select capable men from all the people, men who feared God, trustworthy men who hated dishonest gain, and appoint them as officials over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. "Have these men judge the people at all times. Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own, so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you."

Jethro told Moses that if he did this, and God so commanded, Moses would be able to stand the strain, and all these people would go home satisfied. Moses listened to Jethro and did everything he said. He chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads of the people, officials over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They judged the people at all times. The difficult cases they brought to Moses, but the simple ones they decided themselves.
Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own country.
Israel had bread from heaven, water from a rock, victory over Amalek, and judges beside Moses. Ahead of them rose the mountain where the cloud had first spoken to Moses alone.

title: The Mountain and the Covenant
subtitle: Exodus 19 to 24, Berean Standard Bible
description: Thunder at Sinai, the Ten Commandments, the laws of daily life, and the covenant sealed with blood.
paragraphs: On the first day of the third month after the Israelites left Egypt, they entered the Desert of Sinai and camped in front of the mountain. The runaway shepherd who had once led Jethro's flock to Horeb now stood at that same mountain with a nation at his back.

Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him from the mountain and told him what to say to the house of Jacob and the people of Israel. They had seen what God did to the Egyptians. They had seen how He carried them on eagles' wings and brought them to Himself. "Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations, for the whole earth is Mine. And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation."

Moses came down and summoned the elders. He set before them all the words the LORD had commanded him. "And all the people answered together, 'We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.'" Moses brought their words back to the LORD.

The LORD told Moses He would come to him in a dense cloud, so the people would hear Him speaking with Moses and would always trust him. Moses was to consecrate the people that day and the next. They were to wash their clothes and be ready by the third day, because on the third day the LORD would come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.

Boundaries were set around the mountain. The people were not to go up the mountain or touch its edge. Whoever touched the mountain was to be put to death. No hand was to touch that person. He was to be stoned or shot with arrows, whether man or animal. He was not to live. Only when the ram's horn sounded a long blast could the people approach the mountain.
Moses consecrated the people. They washed their clothes. He told them to be ready by the third day and not to go near a woman.

"On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram's horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled." Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain. Mount Sinai was covered with smoke because the LORD descended on it in fire. The smoke billowed up like smoke from a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled violently. The sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder.

The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses up. Moses went up. The LORD warned him to go down again and warn the people not to force their way through to see the LORD, or many of them would perish. Even the priests, who approached the LORD, had to consecrate themselves, or the LORD would break out against them. Moses answered that the people could not come up because God Himself had warned them to consecrate the mountain and set its boundaries. The LORD told him to go down and bring Aaron up with him, but not to let the priests and people break through. Moses went down and told the people.
Then God spoke the words Israel would carry for the rest of its life.
"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before Me."

They were not to make an idol for themselves, in the form of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. They were not to bow down to idols or worship them, for the LORD their God is a jealous God, punishing the children for the sin of the parents to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Him, but showing love to a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments.
"You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain."

"Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy." Six days they were to labor and do all their work. The seventh day was a Sabbath to the LORD their God. On it they were not to do any work, neither they, nor sons or daughters, nor male or female servants, nor animals, nor any foreigner residing in their towns. In six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but He rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
"Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you."
"You shall not murder."
"You shall not commit adultery."
"You shall not steal."
"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor."
"You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor."

When the people saw the thunder and lightning, heard the trumpet, and saw the mountain in smoke, they trembled with fear and stayed at a distance. They said to Moses that he should speak to them, and they would listen. They did not want God to speak to them, or they would die. Moses told them not to be afraid. God had come to test them, so that the fear of God would be with them to keep them from sinning. The people remained at a distance while Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.

The laws that followed filled the space between God's mountain and Israel's daily life. They covered altars and idols, servants and violence, injury and repayment, theft and lost property, loans and pledges, the stranger, the widow, the orphan, the poor, and the rest owed to people, animals, and land.

Some laws were hard. A Hebrew servant bought by an Israelite was to serve six years and go free in the seventh without paying anything. Rules governed a daughter sold as a servant, a wife's food, clothing, and marital rights, and what happened when masters injured the people under their power. A man who willfully attacked another and killed him was to be put to death, but a man whose killing was not premeditated could flee to a place God appointed. A man who struck his father or mother was to be put to death. A kidnapper was to be put to death. Anyone who cursed father or mother was to be put to death. Injuries were to be measured and repaid with care: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise. An owner whose ox gored a man or woman to death faced judgment, and the ox was to be stoned.

Other laws reached into the ordinary corners of the camp. A thief caught breaking in had different consequences by night and by day. A man who stole an ox or sheep and slaughtered or sold it had to pay back five cattle for the ox and four sheep for the sheep. A man who borrowed an animal answered for it under set terms. A man who seduced a virgin who was not pledged in marriage had to marry her and pay the bride price, unless her father refused to give her to him, and then he still had to pay. A sorceress was not to be allowed to live. Anyone who had sexual relations with an animal was to be put to death. Anyone who sacrificed to any god other than the LORD was to be destroyed.

God also bound Israel's memory to its mercy. "You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt." "You must not mistreat any widow or orphan." If a widow or orphan cried out to God, God would hear their cry. "If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest." If a neighbor's cloak was taken as a pledge, it was to be returned by sunset, because the cloak was the only covering he had for his body. If he cried out to God, God would hear, for God is compassionate.

Justice had rules too. The Israelites were not to spread false reports or help a guilty man by being a malicious witness. They were not to follow the crowd in doing wrong or pervert justice by siding with the crowd. They were not to show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit or deny justice to a poor man because he was poor. They were to keep far from false charges and not kill the innocent or righteous. They were not to accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the innocent. Even an enemy's ox or donkey wandering away was to be taken back. Even an enemy's animal fallen under its load was not to be left without help.

Rest ran through the laws as well as through the week. For six years Israel sowed the land and gathered its produce. In the seventh year the land was to lie unplowed and unused so the poor among the people could get food from it, and wild animals could eat what was left. The same was to be done with vineyards and olive groves. "For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident."

Three times a year all the men were to appear before the Sovereign LORD: at the Festival of Unleavened Bread, which remembered the month Israel came out of Egypt; at the Festival of Harvest, with the firstfruits of the crops sown in the field; and at the Festival of Ingathering at the end of the year, when the crops were gathered from the field.

God promised to send an angel ahead of Israel to guard them along the way and bring them to the place He had prepared. Israel was to pay attention to him and listen to what he said. They were not to rebel against him. If Israel obeyed God's voice and did all He said, God would be an enemy to their enemies and oppose those who opposed them. They were not to bow down to the gods of the nations ahead or serve them. They were to serve the LORD their God, and He would bless their bread and water and take sickness away from them. God would drive out the nations little by little, not in a single year, lest the land become desolate and the wild animals become too many. He would set Israel's borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the Euphrates River.
After Moses gave the people these words, he went and told them all the words and ordinances of the LORD. "They all responded with one voice: 'All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.'"

Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Early the next morning he got up and built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars representing the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent young Israelite men to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as fellowship offerings to the LORD. Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins. The other half he splashed against the altar. Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people. They responded that all the LORD had said they would do, and they would obey. "So Moses took the blood, splattered it on the people, and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.'"

Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up and saw the God of Israel. "Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself." God did not raise His hand against these leaders of the Israelites. They saw God, and they ate and drank.

The LORD told Moses to come up to Him on the mountain and stay there. He would give him the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments He had written for their instruction. Moses set out with Joshua, his aide. He told the elders to wait there until he and Aaron came back. If anyone had a dispute, he could go to Aaron and Hur, who were with the elders.

When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it. The glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered the mountain. On the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud. To the Israelites, the glory of the LORD looked like a consuming fire on top of the mountain. "Moses entered the cloud as he went up on the mountain, and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights."
Below the cloud, the camp waited with the blood of the covenant still fresh in its memory. Above the camp, Moses waited inside the cloud for the words God would place in his hands.

title: Plans for the Dwelling
subtitle: Exodus 25 to 31, Berean Standard Bible
description: The pattern shown on the mountain: the ark, the tent, the priestly garments, and the craftsman God named.
paragraphs: Moses was still on the mountain. Under the cloud, Israel had promised to obey. Inside the cloud, God began to speak about a tent.

The LORD told Moses to tell the Israelites to bring Him an offering. From everyone whose heart prompted him to give, Moses was to receive the offering: gold, silver, and bronze; blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen; goat hair; ram skins dyed red and other durable leather; acacia wood; olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for fragrant incense; onyx stones and other gems to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.

God did not only want gifts. He named the purpose. The Israelites were to make a sanctuary for Him, and He would dwell among them. Moses was to make the tabernacle and all its furnishings exactly like the pattern he was shown on the mountain.
First came the ark.

It was to be made of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. It was to be overlaid with pure gold, inside and out, with a gold molding around it. Four gold rings were to be cast for its feet, two on each side. Poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold were to be made and put through the rings so the ark could be carried. The poles were to stay in the rings. They were not to be removed. Into the ark Moses was to put the testimony God would give him.

On top of the ark God set the mercy seat, a cover of pure gold the same length and width as the ark. Two cherubim of hammered gold were to be made, one at each end of the cover, of one piece with it. The cherubim were to spread their wings upward, overshadowing the cover with their wings. They were to face each other, looking toward the mercy seat. God told Moses He would meet with him there, from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim on the ark of the testimony, and speak with him about all He commanded for Israel.

Then came the table for the Bread of the Presence. It too was acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, with a gold molding, a rim, rings, and poles for carrying. Gold dishes, pans, pitchers, and bowls were to be made for it. The Bread of the Presence was to be set out on the table before God at all times.

Then came the lampstand. It was to be made of pure gold, hammered out: base and shaft, cups, buds, and blossoms all of one piece. Six branches were to extend from its sides, three on one side and three on the other, with almond blossoms on the branches. Seven lamps were to be set upon it so they lit the space in front of it. Its wick trimmers and trays were to be of pure gold. A talent of pure gold was to be used for the lampstand and all these accessories. Moses was warned again: see that he made them according to the pattern shown him on the mountain.

From furniture God moved to the tent itself. The tabernacle was to have ten curtains of finely twisted linen and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim worked into them by a skilled craftsman. The curtains would be joined in two sets of five. Loops and gold clasps would hold them together so the tabernacle would be a unit.

Over those curtains would go a tent of goat hair, eleven curtains in all. Over that would go a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of durable leather. Around the dwelling would stand upright frames of acacia wood, held by silver bases and crossbars overlaid with gold. The tabernacle was to be set up according to the plan shown to Moses on the mountain.

Inside the tent, a veil mattered more than the walls. It was to be made of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen, with cherubim worked into it by a skilled craftsman. It would hang on gold hooks set on acacia posts overlaid with gold and standing on silver bases. The veil was to separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. The ark of the testimony was to be placed behind it, and the mercy seat was to be set on top of the ark in the Most Holy Place. The table was to stand outside the veil on the north side, and the lampstand opposite it on the south side. For the entrance to the tent, a curtain of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen, the work of an embroiderer, would hang on five posts with gold hooks and bronze bases.

Outside, an altar waited. It was to be made of acacia wood, square, five cubits long and five cubits wide and three cubits high. Horns were to be made on its four corners, of one piece with the altar, and it was to be overlaid with bronze. Its pots for removing ashes, shovels, basins for sprinkling, meat forks, and firepans were to be bronze. A bronze grating would sit inside it, with bronze rings and poles for carrying. The altar was to be hollow, made with planks, just as Moses was shown on the mountain.

Around the tabernacle would stand a courtyard, a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely twisted linen on posts with bronze bases and silver hooks and bands. The entrance curtain would be twenty cubits wide, worked in the same blue, purple, and scarlet pattern. Clear oil from pressed olives was to be brought so the lamps could burn continually. In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that was before the testimony, Aaron and his sons were to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This was to be a lasting ordinance for the generations to come.
Then God set apart the men who would serve at the altar.

Moses was to bring Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water. Sacred garments were to be made for Aaron, for glory and for beauty. God named their parts in detail: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. Wise men, filled by God with a spirit of wisdom, were to make them so Aaron could be consecrated to serve as priest.

The ephod was to be made of gold and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen, the work of a skilled craftsman. Its shoulder pieces would carry two onyx stones set in gold filigree, engraved with the names of the sons of Israel, six on one stone and six on the other, in the order of their birth. Aaron would bear their names on his shoulders before the LORD as a memorial.

The breastpiece of judgment was to be made in the same colors and workmanship. It would be square and folded double. Four rows of precious stones would be mounted on it, three in each row, twelve stones in all, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes. It would be attached to the ephod and worn over Aaron's heart whenever he entered the Holy Place. Aaron would bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart before the LORD continually. The Urim and the Thummim were also to be put in the breastpiece, so Aaron would bear the means of making decisions for the Israelites over his heart before the LORD.

The robe of the ephod was to be made entirely of blue cloth. Around its hem were to be pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with gold bells between them. The sound of the bells would be heard when Aaron entered the Holy Place before the LORD and when he came out, so that he would not die. A plate of pure gold was to be made and engraved like a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD. It would be fastened with a blue cord to the front of the turban. Aaron would wear it on his forehead continually, bearing the guilt connected with the sacred gifts Israel offered, so they might be acceptable before the LORD.

The consecration of Aaron and his sons would take seven days. A young bull and two rams without defect were to be brought. Unleavened bread and cakes and wafers without yeast would be placed in a basket. Aaron and his sons would be washed, dressed, and anointed. The bull would be slaughtered as a sin offering. Blood would be put on the horns of the altar and poured out at its base. One ram would be offered whole as a burnt offering. The other ram, the ram of ordination, would be slaughtered, and its blood put on the tip of Aaron's right ear, on the tips of his sons' right ears, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet, with blood splashed against the sides of the altar. Anointing oil and altar blood would be sprinkled on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments. They would be consecrated. Portions of the ordination ram and bread would be waved before the LORD and eaten by Aaron and his sons at the entrance of the tent of meeting. For seven days the process would be repeated, and the altar would be made holy through atonement.

Every day after that, two lambs a year old were to be offered regularly. One lamb would be offered in the morning and the other at twilight, with flour mixed with oil and a drink offering of wine. This burnt offering would stand at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, where God promised to meet His people and speak to Moses. The place would be consecrated by God's glory.

"Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God. And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God."

God planned more furniture and more fragrance. The altar of incense was to be made of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, with a horn at each corner, rings for poles, and a place before the veil that was before the ark of the testimony. Aaron was to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tended the lamps and again at twilight when he lit them, so incense would burn regularly before the LORD for generations. No unauthorized incense was to be offered there, and no burnt offering, grain offering, or drink offering was to be poured on it. Once a year Aaron was to make atonement on its horns with blood from the sin offering of atonement. It was most holy to the LORD.

When a census was taken, each man counted was to give a ransom for his life to the LORD, half a shekel according to the sanctuary shekel. Rich and poor would give the same amount. The atonement money from the Israelites was to be appointed for the service of the tent of meeting, as a memorial before the LORD. A bronze basin on a bronze stand was to be placed between the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron and his sons were to wash their hands and feet with water from it whenever they entered the tent of meeting or approached the altar to minister, so they would not die.

The anointing oil itself was holy. It would be mixed by a skilled perfumer from liquid myrrh, cinnamon, fragrant cane, cassia, and olive oil, according to exact amounts. With it Moses was to anoint the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony, the table and all its articles, the lampstand and its accessories, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. Whatever touched them would become holy. Aaron and his sons were to be anointed and consecrated to serve as priests. The oil was not to be poured on anyone else's body, and Israel was not to make any like it for common use. It was sacred. Incense too was given a pure formula of spices, blended by a perfumer, salted, pure, and sacred. It was not to be made for private use. Whoever made any like it to enjoy its fragrance was to be cut off from his people.

God then named the chief craftsman. He had chosen Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. "And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship," to make artistic designs in gold, silver, and bronze, to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts. God also appointed Oholiab, son of Ahisamak, of the tribe of Dan, to help him. And God gave ability to all the skilled workers, so they would make everything commanded: the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony with its mercy seat, all the furnishings, the table and its articles, the pure gold lampstand and all its accessories, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, the basin with its stand, the woven garments for Aaron and his sons, the anointing oil, and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They were to make them just as God commanded.

Above all the skill still stood the Sabbath. The Israelites were to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations as a lasting covenant. It was a sign between God and Israel forever, for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed. Anyone who desecrated the Sabbath was to be put to death. Anyone who did any work on it was to be cut off from among his people. Six days work could be done, but the seventh was a day of Sabbath rest, holy to the LORD.
"When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God."
Moses held God's words on stone. Below the mountain, the camp was still waiting, and the waiting was about to turn.

title: The Golden Calf
subtitle: Exodus 32 to 34, Berean Standard Bible
description: The golden calf, Moses’ intercession, God’s name proclaimed on the mountain, and Moses returning with a radiant face.
paragraphs: When the people saw that Moses was so long in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron.
They told him to make them gods who would go before them. As for this fellow Moses who had brought them up out of Egypt, they did not know what had happened to him.

Aaron told them to take off the gold earrings their wives, sons, and daughters were wearing and bring them to him. The people took off their gold earrings and brought them to Aaron. "He took the gold from their hands, and with an engraving tool he fashioned it into a molten calf. And they said, 'These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!'"

When Aaron saw this, he built an altar in front of the calf and announced that tomorrow there would be a festival to the LORD. The next day the people rose early and sacrificed burnt offerings and presented fellowship offerings. Afterward they sat down to eat and drink and got up to play.

On the mountain, the LORD told Moses to go down, because the people he had brought up out of Egypt had become corrupt. They had been quick to turn away from what God commanded them. They had made themselves an idol cast in the shape of a calf. They had bowed down to it, sacrificed to it, and credited it with bringing them up out of Egypt.
God called them a stiff-necked people. His anger burned. He told Moses to leave Him alone, so that His anger might burn against them and consume them, and He would make Moses into a great nation.

Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God. He asked why God's anger should burn against His own people, whom He had brought out of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand. Why should the Egyptians be able to say that God brought Israel out with evil intent to kill them in the mountains and wipe them off the face of the earth? Moses pleaded with God to turn from His fierce anger and relent. He asked Him not to bring disaster on His people. He called on God to remember His servants Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom God had sworn by Himself that He would make their descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and give them all the land He had promised as their inheritance forever.
Then the LORD relented and did not bring on His people the disaster He had threatened.

Moses turned and went down the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hands. They were inscribed on both sides, front and back. The tablets were the work of God. The writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.

As Moses and Joshua came close to the camp, Joshua heard the sound of the people shouting. He told Moses there was the sound of war in the camp. Moses answered that it was not the sound of victory or defeat. It was the sound of singing he heard.
"As Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain."
